title: Stall detection & replaybench — ingress/egress streaming latency (Apr 2026)
content:
Summary:

This is a working note for a small exploratory benchmark ("replaybench") and instrumentation approach intended to isolate transient stalls and microbursts that increase tail latency for streaming LLM responses. The goal: reproducible, low-effort experiment that: (1) detects short-lived stalls at ingress/egress hops, (2) measures how different transports and chunking strategies amplify or attenuate those stalls, and (3) determines action levers we can implement in the serving runtime and edge proxies.

Motivation / scope:

- We've repeatedly observed small (2–30ms) pauses during streaming traffic that disproportionately increase 99.9th latency for token delivery.
- Existing telemetry (per-request p50/p95 token latency) hides these microstalls; trace spans are coarse.
- Hypothesis: specific combinations of client flush patterns, proxy buffering, and transport flow-control cause transient head-of-line stalls that cascade into application-level stalls.
- This doc focuses on networking/transport-level causes (not model compute).

Testbed (hardware & config):

- Client runner: 3x t3.medium-like instances (simulated clients) running parallel streams via our SDK streaming client patched to allow deterministic flush patterns.
- Edge hop: Envoy 1.24 pinned with our standard front-proxy config (custom filter chain).
- Middle proxy: haproxy in some runs (to compare simplistic buffer semantics).
- Backend: dev serving runtime (single GPU worker) on g5.xlarge-equivalent; model stub that emits tokens at a controlled pace (to separate compute variance).
- Network: NIC shaping to 50Mbps and artificially inject 0–50ms variable latency using tc/netem; optional per-flow queuing to emulate cloud LB jitter.

Key differences vs prior probes:

- We use deterministic "flush scripts" that instruct client to send X bytes then pause for Y ms before next flush. This lets us emulate real app flush patterns (e.g., prompt then user stream).
- We implement replaybench: capture a real production ingress trace (size/timing of application writes) and replay at variable compression and socket pacing settings.
- We record micro-timestamps at five handoff points (client socket write, proxy recv, proxy forward, backend recv, backend app-ack/emit). Time sync via monotonic counters and a small alignment handshake.

Measurements and signal capture:

- Sampled traces: when any stream crosses token-emit > 50ms past previous token we mark as a microstall event.
- Metrics per stream: token inter-arrival CDF, microstall count per 1k tokens, max stall length, sum-of-stalls (ms), and stall-induced token backlog.
- Aggregate metrics: p50/p95/p99/p99.9 for inter-token latency and stall rates.

Methodology overview (repro steps):

1) Capture production-ish trace: "prod-flush-20260314" (10k tokens across 1000 streams) using lightweight capture hook on SDK.
2) Normalise payload sizes and remove auth noise; keep per-write flush timings.
3) Replay with four transport modes:
   - HTTP/1.1 chunked + keep-alive
   - HTTP/2 streaming (single stream, default flow-control)
   - gRPC bidi streaming (grpc-go default; with flow-control tweaks)
   - HTTP/1.1 with manual application-level framing (explicit small frames to avoid chunk coalescing)
4) For each transport, run 3 scenarios:
   A) baseline (no induced network jitter)
   B) jitter (uniform 0–25ms random latency + 1% 50–100ms spikes)
   C) proxy-buffered (Envoy configured to enable downstream buffering with small window)
5) Repeat runs with socket-level Nagle disabled/enabled and TLS record sizing varied (small 512B vs large 16KB).

Representative commands (dev):

- trace capture: ./sdk-capture --streams 1000 --duration 300s --out prod-flush-20260314.json
- replay: ./replaybench --input prod-flush-20260314.json --transport http2 --jitter 0-25 --spike 1%:100ms --tls-record 512 --nagle off
- tracer: tracer-agent --writepoints client,edge,backend --out csv

Experimental notes & quick findings (raw):

- HTTP/1.1 chunk coalescing + Envoy buffering produced the most pronounced long-tail: many microstalls of 10–40ms that correlated with proxy flush cycles.
- HTTP/2 flow-control stalls were rare except when combined with server-side blocking writes (application paused >50ms), which then created head-of-line that affected all streams multiplexed on the same connection.
- gRPC showed an interesting failure mode: when the client flush pattern had bursts followed by long pauses, flow-control ACK pacing from server to client caused bursts of up-to-3x token delay variability compared to HTTP/1.1 framed runs.
- Disabling Nagle improved median inter-token latency by ~2ms in low-bandwidth runs but increased packet count and slightly increased jitter at the edge.
- Small TLS record sizes (512B) reduced coalescing-caused stalls but caused more CPU overhead and slightly higher p50.

Ascii results snapshot (one run, baseline vs jitter vs proxy-buffered, http1-chunked):

Mode           p50(ms)  p95(ms) p99(ms) p99.9(ms) microstall/1k tokens
baseline       9        18      35      72       3.2
jitter         11       28      65      134      9.7
proxy-buffered 13       42      180     410      28.4

What the traces showed (examples):

- Example trace A: client wrote 4 small flushes (200–400B) spaced 8ms apart. Envoy buffered and forwarded as a single 3KB write; backend consumed first chunk and stalled 12ms waiting for more bytes -> resulting in 12ms microstall at token 4. Without buffering, tokens flowed with 6–9ms intervals.
- Example trace B: HTTP/2 multiplexing: stream A blocks in server write for 60ms. Because connection window had been consumed by large requests on other streams, the server couldn't push new frames for stream A until windows were replenished -> correlated p99 jump for unrelated streams on same conn.

Interpretation / root-cause hypotheses:

- Proxy buffering heuristics intended to reduce small writes are trading off decreased wire overhead for increased token latency when upstream emits small frequent writes. The buffer flush interval and downstream congestion interplay is the main culprit in these tests.
- Transport-level flow-control (HTTP/2, gRPC) can transform a single-stream stall in server into a multi-stream degradation due to multiplexing.

Short-term mitigations to try (low-risk):

1) Client-side: expose an SDK option to coalesce up to X bytes or to prefer application-level frame boundaries (force small frames). Make it opt-in for PLG clients where latency matters.
2) Edge config: add a runtime knob to disable Envoy downstream buffering for streaming routes or set an aggressive max-buffer-bytes low-watermark when route is marked "low-latency".
3) Server-side: warn when server write stalls > 30ms and emit a metric to the request-level trace so SRE can correlate with flow-control backpressure.
4) Canary: a config that pins streaming traffic to separate HTTP/2 connections per high-QPS customer to reduce multiplex risk (costly but for enterprise tier only).

Longer-term changes (investigate):

- Implement a replaybench-based synthetic alert: when production trace replay shows >X microstalls/1k tokens we auto-open INF issue with captured traces.
- Investigate adaptive TLS record sizing in the runtime: choose record size based on recent token size distribution to minimize coalescing.
- Consider adding a small push-based heartbeat from server to avoid flow-control window starvation when application stalls briefly (careful: must not increase bandwidth for normal flows).

Open questions / unknowns:

- How often do these patterns show up in real customer traffic vs our synthetic trace? Need sampling across multiple customer workloads.
- Does separating streaming traffic onto separate connections materially increase cost or management complexity?
- Which of these mitigations can be turned on by default without breaking client integrations?

Action items (next week):

- [Priya] Run replaybench across three production captures from different customers and summarize stall rates by transport (due 2026-04-30).
- [Miguel] Prototype Envoy route-level "disable_downstream_buffering" config and measure CPU/throughput impact (due 2026-05-04).
- [Lina] Add server-side write stall metric and a simple alert rule in dev (due 2026-04-29).
- [Owen] Run cost estimate for per-customer HTTP/2 connection pinning (due 2026-05-07).

Notes to self / TODOs for doc:

- Add diagrams showing the five handoff counters and an example flame of a microstall.
- Attach raw CSV traces for the three representative runs.
- Convert replaybench runner into a reproducible GH action for nightly runs.

If anyone wants to reproduce quickly: ping #eng-serving-runtime and I will drop the prod-flush-20260314 capture and a docker-compose to run the exact testbed.

End of note.
